items: Understand how technical Solution Architect interviews differ from coding interviews.
Practice structured, discussion-style answers to realistic architecture scenarios.
Use the Well-Architected lens (cost, reliability, security, ops, performance, sustainability) to frame every answer.
Communicate trade-offs clearly instead of claiming a single "correct" design.

blocks.text: A technical Solution Architect interview is rarely a coding test. Instead, it is a conversation at the whiteboard (physical or shared, e.g. Miro/Excalidraw) where the interviewer throws a realistic, ambiguous problem at you and watches how you think. They are assessing five things:

items: Breadth vs. depth — can you name the relevant patterns, then go deep where it matters?
Trade-off reasoning — do you justify a choice with why, and what you gave up?
Pragmatism — do you reach for the simplest thing that meets the NFRs, not the trendiest?
Communication — can a non-specialist follow your diagram and narrative?
Curiosity & pushback — do you ask clarifying questions before designing?

blocks.text: Format tip: Open every answer with 2–3 clarifying questions. Silence the urge to "just start drawing." Interviewers score the scoping as much as the solution.

The rest of this lesson is a set of mock scenarios in the style of jassics/security-interview-questions' "Security Architect Scenario Questions," but re-themed for Solution Architecture. Each scenario has a realistic prompt, a structured MODEL ANSWER (bullets with Tools: / Techniques: / Output: sub-bullets), and an Interviewer listens for note.
Scenario 1 — Migrating a 15-Year-Old Monolith to Cloud-Native
Prompt: "You're asked to migrate a 15-year-old monolith — a core ERP system — to a cloud-native architecture. Walk me through your approach."

items: Inventory the monolith: modules, dependencies, data stores, peak load, compliance constraints.
Map to the 7R strategies (Rehost, Replatform, Refactor, Rearchitect, Repurchase, Retain, Retire).
Classify each module's business criticality and change frequency.
Techniques: dependency mapping, event storming, DORA/health metrics baseline.
Tools: AWS Migration Evaluator, vFunction, static analysis (SonarQube), CMDB.
Output: a migration wave plan with R-decisions per capability.
Apply the Strangler Fig pattern: stand up an API facade/edge in front of the monolith and route one capability at a time to a new service.
Keep the monolith as the source of truth until each seam is extracted and verified.
Techniques: Branch by Abstraction, parallel run, shadow traffic.
Tools: API Gateway, feature flags (LaunchDarkly), service mesh (for gradual cutover).
Output: a strangler routing map and per-wave acceptance criteria.
Identify bounded contexts (e.g., Billing, Inventory, HR) to avoid a "distributed monolith."
Each context owns its data (Database-per-Service).
Techniques: context mapping, anti-corruption layer between legacy and new.
Output: bounded-context map and the first 1–2 candidate services to extract.
Don't lift the 15-year-old schema wholesale. Use Change Data Capture (CDC) to sync legacy DB → new service DB during transition.
Techniques: dual-write with reconciliation, strangler at the data layer.
Tools: Debezium, AWS DMS.
Output: data sync pipeline + reconciliation report.
Pick the lowest-risk, highest-learnings capability first (a "learning wave").
Wrap with resilience (Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead) at the gateway boundary.
Output: a measured pilot that de-risks the rest of the program.
Discovery & portfolio classification (don't start moving code yet)
Choose an incremental path, not a big-bang rewrite
Define target boundaries with DDD
Modernize data separately
Prove it with a pilot wave
Did they resist the "rewrite everything" temptation? (Maturity signal.)
Do they mention strangler/7R/DDD specifically, not just "we'll use microservices"?
Do they separate application migration from data migration?
Trade-off awareness: speed (rehost) vs. long-term value (rearchitect).

blocks.text: Scenario 2 — Resilience Strategy for a Payments Service
Prompt: "Design a resilience strategy for a payments service that must stay available even when downstream banks are slow or down."

items: Give payments its own thread/connection pool and its own deployment so a noisy neighbor can't starve it.
Techniques: separate resource pools, dedicated autoscaling group/namespace.
Tools: Hystrix/Resilience4j, Kubernetes resource quotas, separate node pools.
Output: isolated payment workload with bounded blast radius.
Wrap every bank call with a timeout and a circuit breaker; fail fast when the bank is unhealthy.
Techniques: half-open probing, exponential backoff + jitter on retry (idempotent only).
Tools: Resilience4j, Envoy/Linkerd sidecar, API Gateway policies.
Output: breaker config (threshold, cool-down) and timeout budget.
A payment is a distributed transaction: authorize → capture → settle. Use an orchestrated Saga with compensating actions.
Techniques: state machine orchestrator, idempotency keys, outbox pattern for reliable events.
Tools: Temporal/Camunda, event bus (Kafka), DB outbox.
Output: saga definition with compensations and a dead-letter path.
If a bank is down, accept the payment asynchronously (queue it) and reconcile later rather than rejecting the user.
Techniques: queue + idempotent retry, eventual consistency with a ledger.
Tools: Kafka/RabbitMQ, a reconciliation batch job.
Output: "accepted, settling" UX + reconcile report.
SLOs for payment success rate, p99 latency; alert on breaker trips and DLQ depth.
Techniques: RED/USE metrics, golden signals, chaos testing the bank dependency.
Tools: Prometheus/Grafana, OpenTelemetry, Chaos Mesh/Litmus.
Output: SLO dashboard + game-day results.
Isolate failure domains with Bulkhead
Stop cascading failures with Circuit Breaker + Timeout
Keep the money safe with Saga (orchestration)
Degrade gracefully with Fallback & Asynchronous reconciliation
Observe everything
Do they treat payments as eventually consistent with compensations, not as a naive ACID transaction?
Is the user experience during partial failure considered (async accept vs. hard fail)?
Do they mention idempotency (double-charge avoidance)?
Do they test failure (chaos) rather than assume it works?

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant P as Payment Service
    participant B as Circuit Breaker
    participant Bank as Bank API
    participant Q as Settlement Queue
    U->>P: Pay(order)
    P->>B: call Bank
    alt Bank healthy
        B->>Bank: authorize+capture
        Bank-->>P: ok
        P-->>U: success
    else Bank down/slow
        B-->>P: open (fail fast)
        P->>Q: enqueue (async settle)
        P-->>U: accepted, settling

blocks.text: Prompt: "How would you choose between orchestration and choreography for a distributed transaction spanning 4 services?"

items: Orchestration = central coordinator drives steps + compensations. Easy to trace, debug, and enforce. Cost: a central component (though it can be highly available).
Choreography = services react to events, no coordinator. Maximal decoupling and no central failure point. Cost: harder to reason about, trace, and version; risk of event spaghetti.
Techniques: draw both on the whiteboard before choosing.
Output: a one-line recommendation with rationale.
Complexity & criticality: for money/movement flows (payments, orders), prefer orchestration — you want a clear audit trail and easy compensation.
Team autonomy & scale: for many independent teams reacting to the same event, choreography reduces coordination overhead.
Observability maturity: if you lack distributed tracing, orchestration is safer.
Tools: Temporal/Camundi (orchestration); Kafka + schema registry (choreography).
Output: a fit-for-purpose choice, not an ideology.
Orchestrate the critical core saga; let non-critical side-effects (notify, analytics) be choreographed events off the saga.
Techniques: saga emits a "OrderCompleted" event; downstream listeners choreograph.
Output: a clean core + loosely-coupled periphery.
State the trade-off explicitly
Decision drivers
Hybrid is allowed
Do they reject "microservices must always be choreographed"?
Do they tie the choice to observability and criticality, not fashion?
Do they recognize a hybrid is often best?

blocks.text: Scenario 4 — Monolith to Microservices: When NOT To
Prompt: "A team wants to split their monolith into 40 microservices next quarter. What do you tell them?"

items: Ask: what problem are we solving? Slow deployments? Scaling hotspots? Team boundaries? Microservices are a solution to org/scale problems, not a default.
Techniques: measure deploy frequency, lead time, module coupling (metrics from Module 4.2).
Tools: DORA metrics, Structure101, dependency graphs.
Output: the actual driver, quantified.
40 services with shared DB and tight sync calls = worse than the monolith.
Techniques: modular monolith first; extract only true bounded contexts with independent data.
Output: a phased plan — modular monolith → 3–5 services → expand if justified.
New costs: network latency, distributed transactions, observability, operational toil.
Techniques: TCO comparison, Well-Architected operational-excellence review.
Output: a cost/benefit that the team can't ignore.
Challenge the premise with data
Warn about the distributed-monolith trap
Make the hidden costs explicit
Courage to say "no" or "not yet."
Understanding that microservices are an organizational pattern, not a technical silver bullet.
Awareness of the operational tax.

blocks.text: Prompt: "Design a multi-cloud strategy using Terraform so we're not locked to one vendor, but still move fast."

items: Keep business logic and Kubernetes portable; accept that some services (managed DB, AI) will be provider-specific.
Techniques: abstraction modules, provider-agnostic interfaces, keep state per-account/per-cloud.
Tools: Terraform with provider blocks (aws, azurerm, gcp), Terragrunt for DRY config.
Output: a module layout with clear "portable core" vs "cloud-specific add-ons."
True active-active multi-cloud is expensive. Prefer: primary cloud + disaster-recovery/failover secondary, or per-workload placement.
Techniques: DNS-based failover, object storage replication, GitOps-promoted config.
Tools: Route53/Global LB, Terraform remote state in each cloud, ArgoCD.
Output: a failover topology, not a continuous dual-write nightmare.
Isolate state per environment/cloud; encrypt; lock via backend; CI-gated plans.
Techniques: PR-based terraform plan + policy-as-code.
Tools: Sentinel/OPA, S3/GCS/Azure blob backends, GitHub Actions.
Output: reproducible, auditable infra.
Separate portable from provider-specific
Avoid "worst of both clouds"
Governance & state hygiene
Do they push back on "no lock-in" as an absolute (it has a real cost)?
Do they distinguish portability from active-active?
State management maturity (remote state, locking, policy).

blocks.text: Prompt: "We want to add an AI assistant that answers questions from our internal 50k-document knowledge base. How would you architect it?"

items: Retrieve relevant chunks, augment the prompt, generate. Keeps answers grounded in your docs and auditable.
Techniques: chunking + embeddings, vector similarity search, re-ranking, citation.
Tools: pgvector/Weaviate/Qdrant, embeddings (OpenAI/Cohere/local), LLM API.
Output: RAG pipeline with a grounding/citation step.
Guardrails: PII redaction, prompt-injection defenses, answer groundedness checks (reject if no retrieved context).
Techniques: retrieval confidence threshold, human-in-the-loop for high-risk actions.
Tools: LangChain/LlamaIndex orchestration, guardrail layer, caching of common queries.
Output: a guarded assistant with fallback to "I don't know."
Cache embeddings, cache frequent answers, use smaller models where possible, async re-indexing.
Techniques: embedding cache, semantic cache, batch re-index.
Output: a cost model per 1k queries.
RAG over fine-tuning for fresh, citeable knowledge
Keep it safe and cost-aware
Cost & latency control
RAG vs fine-tune reasoning (freshness, cost, audit).
Do they address hallucination/grounding and cost?
Security: PII, injection, exfiltration.

blocks.value:
flowchart LR
    Q[User Question] --> E[Embed Query]
    E --> V[(Vector Store: 50k docs)]
    V --> R[Retrieve Top-K + Re-rank]
    R --> G[LLM: Augment + Cite]
    G --> A[Answer + Sources]
    G -->|low confidence| F[Fallback: human / I don't know]

blocks.text: Scenario 7 — Cost & Trade-off Analysis Under Constraint
Prompt: "Leadership wants to cut cloud spend 30% without hurting the customer experience. What's your plan?"

items: Attribute cost by service, environment, and tag; find the top contributors.
Techniques: unit economics (cost per transaction), idle-resource detection.
Tools: AWS Cost Explorer/CUR, GCP Billing, Infracost in CI.
Output: a cost heatmap.
Right-size, move dev/test to schedules, use commitments (Savings Plans/Reserved) for stable baselines, delete orphaned storage.
Techniques: autoscaling tuning, spot for batch, storage lifecycle.
Output: a 30% plan with risk labels.
Tie every cut to an SLO; if p99 or error budget degrades, roll back.
Techniques: error-budget policy, canary on infra changes.
Output: a cost plan guarded by SLOs.
Measure before cutting
Target quick, safe wins
Protect experience with SLOs
Do they cut with data and SLOs, not blanket "turn things off"?
FinOps maturity (unit cost, commitments, tagging).

blocks.text: Before your real interview, score yourself 1–5 on each:

items: I open every scenario with clarifying questions (scope, users, NFRs, constraints).
I can name the relevant pattern and explain the trade-off.
I tie decisions to Well-Architected pillars (reliability, cost, security, ops, perf, sustainability).
I produce a clean diagram (Mermaid/whiteboard) early and evolve it.
I explicitly state what I am not doing and why (e.g., not big-bang, not active-active multi-cloud).
I discuss data migration separately from application migration.
I mention observability/metrics as part of any design.
I can justify cost and operational implications of my design.
I stay pragmatic — simplest design that meets NFRs, not the trendiest.
I invite pushback and adapt when the interviewer adds constraints.

blocks.text: Drill: Take any one scenario above, set a 10-minute timer, and voice-record your answer. Then replay and note where you rambled or skipped the trade-off. Repeat weekly.
